# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia, and its incidence and prevalence are increasing in the United States and globally. [1] Stroke prevention is central to AF management. Oral anticoagulation is effective but carries a sustained risk of major and intracranial hemorrhage, and a substantial proportion of eligible patients are never treated or discontinue therapy. The mechanistic basis for percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) was established by the seminal autopsy and surgical observations of Blackshear and Odell, who reported that of 1288 patients with non-rheumatic atrial fibrillation, 221 (17%) had thrombus detected in the left atrium, and of those with atrial thrombus, 201 (91%) had it located within the left atrial appendage. [2] These data identified the appendage as the dominant source of cardioembolism in non-valvular AF and the logical target for mechanical exclusion.

## Pivotal randomized trials versus warfarin

The first randomized evidence came from PROTECT AF, which randomized 707 patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and at least 1 risk factor to either the Watchman device or continued warfarin in a 2:1 ratio. [3] After a mean follow-up of 2.3 years, the event rates of the composite primary efficacy end point of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death were 3.0% and 4.3% per 100 patient-years in the Watchman and warfarin groups, respectively, meeting the criteria for noninferiority. [4] However, an early periprocedural safety hazard—principally pericardial effusion—prompted the U.S. FDA to request a confirmatory trial.

PREVAIL was designed to address these concerns. PREVAIL was a multicenter, 2:1-randomized controlled trial that enrolled 282 patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation and a CHADS2 score ≥2, randomized to the Watchman device or continued warfarin. [5] At 18 months, the first coprimary efficacy endpoint did not achieve the prespecified criteria for noninferiority, a result attributed largely to an unexpectedly low event rate in the warfarin group; importantly, early safety events occurred in 2.2% of the Watchman arm, significantly lower than in PROTECT AF. [5] The longer-term picture was clarified by the 5-year pooled analysis, which demonstrated that LAAC with Watchman provides stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation comparable to warfarin, with additional reductions in major bleeding, particularly hemorrhagic stroke. [6] The complete 5-year PROTECT AF results were also reported separately. [7]

## Patients ineligible for anticoagulation

Because both pivotal trials enrolled anticoagulation-eligible patients, the ASAP study addressed those with contraindications. This was a multicenter, prospective, nonrandomized study of LAA closure with the Watchman device in 150 patients with nonvalvular AF and CHADS2 score ≥1 who were considered ineligible for warfarin. [8] In this cohort, history of hemorrhagic/bleeding tendencies (93%) was the most common reason for warfarin ineligibility, and the observed ischemic stroke rate was substantially lower than expected for aspirin-treated historical controls, supporting LAAC with antiplatelet-only therapy. [8]

## Comparisons with direct oral anticoagulants

As DOACs supplanted warfarin, the relevant comparator shifted. PRAGUE-17 was a randomized noninferiority trial comparing percutaneous LAAC (Watchman or Amulet) with DOACs (95% apixaban) in patients with nonvalvular AF and a history of cardioembolism, clinically-relevant bleeding, or both CHA2DS2-VASc ≥3 and HAS-BLED ≥2. [9] In long-term follow-up, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs for preventing major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events, and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC. [10] A dedicated subanalysis confirmed the favorable nonprocedural bleeding profile. [11]

## Device evolution and head-to-head comparisons

Device iteration has improved outcomes. The single-arm PINNACLE FLX trial of the next-generation Watchman FLX showed a low primary safety event rate of 0.5% and a 100% rate of effective LAA closure at 12 months with peridevice flow < 5 mm. [12] The first large head-to-head device trial, Amulet IDE, randomly assigned (1:1) patients with NVAF at increased risk of stroke to percutaneous implantation with the Amulet occluder or Watchman device, [13] and found the dual-seal Amulet occluder noninferior with respect to safety and effectiveness compared with the single-seal Watchman device, and superior with respect to left atrial appendage occlusion, [13] though procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet occluder and decreased with operator experience. [13]

## LAAC at the time of catheter ablation

The OPTION trial extended the evidence to the ablation population. Researchers randomized 1,360 patients with AF and an elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score to ablation plus LAAC or ablation plus oral anticoagulation; LAAC was performed either concomitant with or sequentially after ablation. [14] LAAC was noninferior to OAC for the composite primary endpoint of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolization and superior for non–procedure-related bleeding. [14]

## Complications and real-world performance

Device-related thrombus (DRT) is a recognized concern, because thrombus may form on the left atrial face of the device and then potentially embolize. [15] In a pooled analysis of clinical-trial cohorts, DRT was relatively uncommon but associated with elevated thromboembolic risk, underscoring the importance of imaging follow-up. [15] Real-world data are reassuring: the NCDR LAAO Registry, which captured a total of 38,158 procedures from 495 hospitals performed by 1,318 physicians between January 2016 and December 2018, [16] showed that patients undergoing commercial Watchman closure were older and at higher thromboembolic and bleeding risk than trial participants, with a mean CHA2DS2-VASc score of 4.6 and a HAS-BLED score of 3, and most had relative or absolute contraindications to anticoagulation. [16]

## Guidelines

Contemporary guidelines endorse a selective role. The 2024 ESC/EACTS guidelines retain the indication for percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion in patients with contraindications for oral anticoagulation, [17] reaffirming that more than 90% of AF-related left atrial thrombi are located within the appendage. [18] The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline provides parallel U.S. recommendations. [19]

## Conclusion

Across more than 15 years of randomized and registry evidence—from PROTECT AF and PREVAIL [3,4,5] through PRAGUE-17 [9,10] and OPTION [14], with iterative device improvement [12,13]—percutaneous LAAC has matured into a guideline-endorsed alternative for stroke prevention, particularly in patients at high bleeding risk or with anticoagulation contraindications [8,17,19]. Ongoing attention to device-related thrombus [15] and operator experience [13] remains essential to optimizing outcomes.
